what: Essent Group insures mortgage lenders against borrowers defaulting. When an American buys a home with a small deposit, the lender requires private mortgage insurance; Essent collects a monthly premium and pays the lender if the loan goes bad. It also reinsures other insurers and runs a title insurance business.
customers: Mortgage lenders and the government-sponsored buyers of mortgages, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, who require insurance on loans with deposits below twenty per cent.
money: Monthly premiums on insurance in force across a large book of American mortgages.
Returns on the invested premium reserves, plus title insurance and reinsurance.
moat: Private mortgage insurance is a licensed business with six main participants, capital requirements set by the government-sponsored enterprises, and pricing driven by proprietary risk models. Once a policy is written it stays in force for years while the borrower pays monthly, so a good year’s underwriting produces income for a decade. The invested reserves earn interest at no additional cost.
risks: This business loses money precisely when house prices fall, which is also when every other financial asset falls — the risk is not diversifiable.
The current book was largely written against house prices at historic highs, so the collateral behind it is at its most expensive.
Credit losses have been almost nonexistent for a decade, which means the reported profitability reflects an unusually benign period.
New insurance written depends on mortgage origination volumes, which have been depressed by high rates.
Eight analysts average a $70.88 target, only 11% above the current price.
opportunities: A net margin of 54.7% and free cash flow of $853.2M on $1.4B of revenue show how profitable this is when losses are low.
The shares trade at about 8.7 times earnings, 6.9 times EV/EBITDA and 6.6 times free cash flow.
Insurance in force generates premiums for years after it is written, so revenue is unusually predictable.
Debt of $531.9M is modest, and the industry’s capital requirements have been materially strengthened since the financial crisis.
Borrowers with low deposits who have since seen their homes appreciate are far less likely to default, which improves the existing book’s quality.
watch: Delinquency rates on insurance in force. Premium income is predictable and losses are not, so the delinquency trend is the only forward-looking number that matters.
view: Mortgage insurance is a business that looks wonderful for a decade and then explains itself in eighteen months. Essent collects monthly premiums, pays almost no claims, earns a 54.7% net margin and trades at 8.7 times earnings — which is either a glaring bargain or exactly what a well-run mortgage insurer looks like shortly before a housing downturn. The entire analytical question is which part of the cycle this is.

What has genuinely changed since the financial crisis is worth giving credit to. Capital requirements set by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are far stricter, the industry’s underwriting models are better, and the loans being insured are documented and verified in ways that 2006 vintages were not. The companies that failed in 2008 failed because they were undercapitalised against mispriced risk, and that specific failure mode has been addressed. Essent carries $532 million of debt, which is modest.

What has not changed is the shape of the risk. Mortgage insurance loses money when house prices fall, which is also when equities fall, credit spreads widen and employment weakens. The risk is not diversifiable and it is not insurable away — it is the business. And the current book was written largely against house prices at historic highs, which means the collateral is at its most expensive point. The offsetting consideration is real: borrowers who bought with small deposits several years ago now have substantial equity from appreciation, and borrowers with equity do not default.

So my reading is that this is a well-capitalised company in an improved industry, earning exceptional returns during a benign period, priced at a multiple that reflects the market’s memory of what happens in a bad one. That is probably about right rather than a mispricing, and eight analysts seeing 11% of upside agrees. Delinquency rates on insurance in force are the only forward-looking number here, and they move before the earnings do. A rise there is not a data point to monitor — it is the signal to act on.
bull: Stricter post-crisis capital rules and better underwriting hold through a mild downturn while accumulated home equity keeps defaults low, and 8.7 times earnings proves too cheap.
bear: House prices fall against a book written at the peak, delinquencies rise, and a business whose risk cannot be diversified takes losses across the whole portfolio at once.
